CIV-NZ.summary: The N'Zi river basin, the largest left-bank tributary of the Bandama, flowing south from the Ferkessédougou area through central Côte d'Ivoire.
CIV-NZ.ecosystem: Forest–savanna transition zone along the N'Zi river and its lowland valleys.
CIV-NZ.livelihoods: Smallholder farming, including lowland and irrigated rice.
CIV-NZ.why_it_matters: Inland valleys support lowland rice farming, but the basin swings between severe low flows and floods.

sources.note: N'Zi is a tributary of the Bandama
Sub-basin of the Bandama; rises near Ferkessédougou, flows north to south; largest left-bank tributary
M'Bahiakro dam serves irrigated rice in the N'Zi basin
Low-flow vulnerability across the watershed; significant recent floods

COL-CUM.summary: A high Andean area of Cumbal municipality in Nariño, near the Ecuador border.
COL-CUM.ecosystem: Andean highlands and páramo around the Cumbal volcano.
COL-CUM.livelihoods: Dairy cattle, potato farming and traditional 'shagra' plots with Andean tubers.
COL-CUM.why_it_matters: Its páramo supplies water, and family plots keep neglected Andean crops such as oca and mashua in use.

sources.note: Municipality in Nariño; town at ~3,172 m; Pasto indigenous homeland; resguardos
Cumbal and Chiles volcanoes; cold and páramo thermal zones
Páramo partly replaced by small family farms for dairy cattle and potato
Páramo as water source ('custodians of water')

ETH-OG.summary: Ethiopia's Omo-Gibe river basin, draining from the southwestern highlands south to Lake Turkana on the Kenya border.
ETH-OG.ecosystem: Highland-to-lowland mosaic of farmland, river corridors and national parks (Omo, Mago).
ETH-OG.livelihoods: Crop–livestock farming; flood-recession farming along the lower Omo.
ETH-OG.why_it_matters: The Omo supplies most of Lake Turkana's water and feeds the Gibe hydropower dams, but land degradation is a key concern.

sources.note: Omo formed by Gibe and Gojeb; flows to Lake Turkana
River passes Mago and Omo National Parks
Lower Omo peoples depend on flood-retreat cultivation
~90% of Lake Turkana inflow; Gibe I/II/III hydropower; overgrazing and deforestation raise silt

IND-CH.summary: Six districts of central India — Jhansi in Uttar Pradesh and Tikamgarh, Chhatarpur, Damoh, Jabalpur and Mandla in Madhya Pradesh — partly within Bundelkhand.
IND-CH.ecosystem: Rainfed cropland, forests and open natural ecosystems on a hot, sub-humid upland.
IND-CH.livelihoods: Rainfed smallholder farming, livestock keeping and use of common lands.
IND-CH.why_it_matters: Rainfed farms and common lands sustain rural livelihoods, but recurrent drought, erratic rainfall and degraded commons strain farming and water.

sources.note: Jhansi, Tikamgarh, Chhatarpur, Damoh are Bundelkhand districts (Mandla and Jabalpur are not)
Bundelkhand agriculture predominantly rainfed
Recurrent drought in Bundelkhand

KEN-LEI.summary: Four Kenyan counties around Nairobi — Kajiado, Kiambu, Machakos and Makueni — including the semi-arid rangelands of southern Kenya.

sources.note: Kajiado/Amboseli rangelands converting to cropland and settlements
Pastoralist rangeland institutions in Kenya
Land-use change, subdivision and drought in Kajiado rangelands

KEN-LVB.summary: Five counties of western Kenya — Kericho, Kisumu, Nandi, Siaya and Vihiga — from the Lake Victoria shore to the tea highlands.
KEN-LVB.ecosystem: Small-farm cropland mosaic, Lake Victoria shoreline and remnant forest.
KEN-LVB.livelihoods: Smallholder maize and beans, sugarcane and tea, and lake fishing.
KEN-LVB.why_it_matters: Small farms and Lake Victoria's fishery support a very dense population, but land degradation and a stressed fishery put both under pressure.

sources.note: Vihiga most densely populated rural area in Kenya; tea
Kakamega maize and sugarcane zones; degradation (Kakamega/Siaya brief)
Smallholder agriculture in West Kenya
Land degradation in Kakamega and Siaya

MEK-3S.summary: The Sekong, Sesan and Srepok river basins, Mekong tributaries shared by Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam.
MEK-3S.ecosystem: Forested uplands, rivers and floodplains, with rice fields and hydropower reservoirs.
MEK-3S.why_it_matters: About 10% of the Mekong watershed but nearly 40% of Lower Mekong fish species, and dams are changing its flows and fisheries.

sources.note: Hydropower dams in the 3S basins
3S = 10% of Mekong watershed, ~40% of LMB fish species; dams reduce fish biodiversity

PER-PCL.summary: Lowland Amazon area around Pucallpa in Ucayali, covering districts of Coronel Portillo and Padre Abad provinces along the Pucallpa–Aguaytía corridor.
PER-PCL.ecosystem: Amazon rainforest, secondary forest, pasture and cropland.
PER-PCL.livelihoods: Cattle ranching, oil palm, cacao, coffee, plantain and fish farming.
PER-PCL.why_it_matters: Amazon forest is being cleared on a frontier driven by pasture and oil palm expansion.

sources.note: Cattle pasture and oil palm in Ucayali
Deforestation drivers around Pucallpa: logging, shifting cultivation, pasture, oil palm

SEN-FK.summary: Fatick Department in west-central Senegal, a Sudano-Sahelian farming area in the former Sine-Saloum region.
SEN-FK.ecosystem: Rainfed cropland with scattered trees, and salt-affected land along the Sine River.
SEN-FK.livelihoods: Rainfed millet and groundnut, livestock, fishing and salt production.
SEN-FK.why_it_matters: Its farmland and trees underpin local food production, but declining rainfall, soil salinization and falling fertility threaten them.

sources.note: Salinization in Fatick / Sine-Saloum (search summary; verify)
Rainfed millet, groundnut, cowpea; sylvopastoral livestock; fishing; saliculture
Salinization, soil fertility decline, rainfall decline since 1970s

TUN-NW.summary: Seven rural sectors of Le Kef and Siliana governorates in semi-arid northwestern Tunisia.
TUN-NW.ecosystem: Rainfed cereal land, olive groves, rangeland and forest patches on erosion-prone hills.
TUN-NW.livelihoods: Small mixed farms: cereals, olives and sheep and goats.
TUN-NW.why_it_matters: Its hills carry cereals, olives and grazing for small farms, but water erosion is stripping their thin soils.

sources.note: Olive and rainfed cereals; erosion
El Kef-Siliana: semi-arid, mixed cereal–tree–small ruminant systems
Water erosion as main degradation

ZWE-MB.summary: Four districts of Zimbabwe's Zambezi Valley — Mbire, Muzarabani, Mount Darwin and Hurungwe — a semi-arid crop, livestock and wildlife landscape.
ZWE-MB.ecosystem: Cropland, shrubland, forest and rivers, alongside wildlife areas.
ZWE-MB.livelihoods: Cotton, sorghum and finger millet farming; cattle and goats.
ZWE-MB.why_it_matters: Farms and wildlife areas share the valley, so crop damage and human–wildlife conflict weigh on both.

sources.note: Cotton, finger millet and sorghum most common in Mbire; conservancies
Shift from cotton to cattle and goats in Mbire (2022 study; verify citation)
